title: Groundwork for Neural Network-Based Specific Emitter Identification Authentication for IoT
objective: To present groundwork for neural network-based specific emitter identification (SEI) on resource-constrained IoT devices using raw IQ streams, with protocols to secure IoT networks
methodology: Neural networks (NNs) are used for specific emitter identification (SEI) by analyzing raw in-phase and quadrature (IQ) streams. Protocols are proposed to secure IoT networks, with a focus on low-latency, lightweight authentication
performance: NN-based SEI algorithms demonstrated feasibility on resource-rich and constrained devices with low latency, but require refinement for large-scale systems due to challenges in handling environmental factors and scalability
limitations: NN-based SEI requires further refinement for large-scale systems, and current methods may be vulnerable to environmental changes affecting RF fingerprints

title: A Self-supervised Framework for Generalized RF Fingerprinting and Zero-shot Anomaly Detection in Dynamic IoT Networks
objective: Address limitations of traditional RF fingerprinting in dynamic IoT networks with limited labeled data, evolving device behavior, and environmental challenges.
methodology: Self-supervised framework combining domain-informed augmentation (DIA), multi-task contrastive pretraining, and shallow-to-medium CNN fine-tuning with optimized contrastive temperature (τ ≈ 0.1) and learning rate (1×10⁻³).
performance: Achieves ~3× faster convergence, 15–40% improved robustness under impairments/drift, 0.95 few-shot accuracy, and ~0.88 anomaly AUC for zero-shot detection.
limitations: Absolute performance remains constrained in extreme impairment scenarios despite semi-supervised learning improvements.

title: NOT MENTIONED
objective: Smart devices face privacy risks from unauthorized access; traditional cryptography-based identification is vulnerable to attacks. Introduces a lightweight CNN-based RFFID method for Zigbee with low power consumption and high accuracy.
methodology: Proposes a lightweight CNN model for radio frequency fingerprinting identification (RFFID) to reduce power consumption and cost while maintaining high accuracy.
dataset: 4 Zigbee devices with 60,000 samples each (1000 sampling points per sample).
performance: Achieved 100% accuracy in Zigbee device identification and reduced parameters by 93%.
limitations: Relies on hardware-specific RF characteristics, which may limit generalizability.

title: Radio Transmitter Fingerprinting: A Steady State Frequency Domain Approach
objective: Identify radio transmitters via RF fingerprinting for applications like femto base station authentication, addressing challenges in accurate identification and reducing signaling traffic in cellular networks.
methodology: Combines frequency domain analysis with k-NN classifiers to exploit steady-state signal features. Uses USRP transmitters to capture and analyze preambles, normalizing time-domain samples and extracting log-spectral-energy features.
dataset: Eight identical USRP transmitters tested at 30dB and 0dB SNR. Preambles from UMTS RACH channels with 1MHz bandwidth and 4096 chips at 0.768Mcps.
performance: Achieves high accuracy with low-cost receivers; outperforms transient analysis methods by avoiding high sample rate requirements. Accuracy at 30dB SNR (97%), Accuracy at 0dB SNR (66%), k-NN classification performance.
limitations: Transient analysis requires high sample rates and sophisticated receivers. Distinguishing identical transmitters may be challenging without steady-state features.

title: Improving Wireless Network Security Based On Radio Fingerprinting
objective: Enhance wireless network security through hardware-based physical-layer security using radio frequency fingerprinting for device identification.
methodology: Fractional Fourier Transform (FrFT) for transient signal feature extraction, Robust Principal Component Analysis (RPCA) for dimensionality reduction, and K-Nearest Neighbor (KNN) for classification.
dataset: 10 Motorola walkie-talkies for signal collection and identification.
performance: Achieved 100% recognition rate at 20dB SNR with FrFT order 0.8, showing improved performance with increasing SNR.
limitations: Relies on hardware-specific transient signals; potential vulnerabilities in FrFT processing under noisy conditions.
